description: Original paraphrase reference for two-player standard Cribbage plus three common variants (Muggins, shorter 61-point game, skunk rule). Rules, scoring atoms, board mechanics, worked examples, and variant notes only. No verbatim publisher prose is redistributed.
coverage_boundary: Covers two-player standard Cribbage to 121 points, plus Muggins, shorter 61-point game, and skunk-rule variants. Includes rule paraphrases, scoring atoms, board mechanics, worked examples, and variant notes. Cribbage is a public-domain game; the linked source is a widely published English reference, not an official publisher rulebook.

default_source.title: How to Play Cribbage
default_source.permission_note: The game itself is public domain. Only original paraphrases and structured metadata are stored. No verbatim publisher prose is redistributed.

editions.notes: The two-player game as most commonly published in English-language references; game ends at 121 points.

editions.scope: Muggins scoring option layered on the standard game
editions.notes: Opponents may claim any points a player misses when counting their hand or crib. Standard in most competitive play; must be agreed to before the game.

editions.scope: short game to 61 points (once around the board)
editions.notes: Game length reduced to 61. All other mechanics from the standard game apply.

editions.scope: skunk (loser under 91) and double-skunk (loser under 61) game-value multipliers
editions.notes: Multiplies the game value at final scoring based on how far behind the loser is. Must be agreed to before the game.

entries.title: Deck and card rank in two-player Cribbage
entries.summary: Cribbage uses a standard 52-card pack with no jokers. Kings rank highest and Aces rank lowest for the purposes of runs; the Ace never wraps around to link with the King.

entries.title: Choosing the first dealer
entries.summary: Before the first hand, both players cut the deck; whoever draws the lower card deals first. Ties are broken by re-drawing. In a subsequent game the loser of the previous game deals first.

entries.title: The deal: six cards each
entries.summary: The dealer deals six cards face-down to each player, one at a time, starting with the opponent.

entries.title: Forming the crib
entries.summary: Each player looks at their six cards and lays two face-down toward the dealer, keeping four in hand. Those four discarded cards together form the four-card crib. The crib belongs to the dealer and is set aside untouched until it is counted last, after both players' hands.

entries.title: The starter card and 'His Heels'
entries.summary: After the crib is laid away, the non-dealer cuts the remaining deck and the dealer turns up the top card of the lower packet as the starter. If the starter is a Jack, the dealer immediately pegs 2 points, called 'His Heels' (or 'His Nibs' in some references). The starter is not played to the tabletop during the play phase but does count as a fifth card in every hand and in the crib when they are scored.

entries.title: Object of the game
entries.summary: The first player to reach 121 points wins. The game ends the instant that threshold is crossed, whether the crossing happens during pegging in the play phase or while counting a hand or the crib.

entries.title: The play: leading and the running total
entries.summary: Non-dealer leads; the players then alternate playing one card face-up in front of themselves and calling the new running total aloud. The running total may never exceed 31. Face cards each count 10 toward the total, number cards count their pip value, and Aces count 1.

entries.title: 'Go' and reaching exactly 31
entries.summary: If a player cannot add a card without pushing the running total past 31, they say 'Go' and the opponent pegs 1 for the Go. If the opponent can still play cards under 31 they do so before the reset. Landing on exactly 31 scores 2 (instead of 1 for the Go). Whoever plays the last card of a subsequence (that does not reach 31) also pegs 1 for the Go. After a Go or a 31, the count resets to zero and the player who did not play the last card leads next.

entries.title: Pegging: making 15 during the play
entries.summary: If a card played brings the running total to exactly 15, the player who played it pegs 2 points.

entries.title: Pegging: pairs, triplets, and four of a kind
entries.summary: Matching the rank of the last card played scores 2 for a pair, 6 for a third card of the same rank in a row (triplet / pair royal), and 12 for a fourth in a row (double pair royal). Pairs match by rank only: a Jack pairs another Jack but does not pair a Queen even though both count 10 toward the running total.

entries.title: Pegging: runs and the 'foreign card' rule
entries.summary: A run during the play is a stretch of three or more of the most recently played cards whose ranks (ignoring suit) form a consecutive sequence, in any order. A run of three pegs 3, a run of four pegs 4, and so on. The sequence is broken as soon as an unrelated 'foreign' card is played into it. So 8-7-7-6 does not form a run (the second 7 is foreign), but 9-6-8-7 does form a run of four because the last four cards can be rearranged into 6-7-8-9.

entries.title: Counting order and the five-card hand
entries.summary: After the play ends, the hands and crib are counted in this fixed order: non-dealer's hand first, then dealer's hand, then the dealer's crib last. Each of the three is scored as a five-card set: the four cards from the player's hand (or the crib) combined with the same starter card. The starter therefore contributes to all three counts.

entries.title: Counting: fifteens and pairs in the show
entries.summary: Every distinct combination of cards from the five-card set that sums to 15 counts 2 points, and every distinct pair (two cards of the same rank) counts 2 points. Combinations are counted separately, so the same card can participate in more than one fifteen or pair.

entries.title: Counting: runs in the show
entries.summary: A run in the show is three or more cards whose ranks form a consecutive sequence (order irrelevant). Each run counts 1 point per card. Ace is always low; there is no wrap from King back to Ace. If the same run appears more than once because a rank in it is duplicated, each distinct version is scored — see the 'common formulas' entry.

entries.title: Counting: flush rules for hand and crib
entries.summary: A hand flush requires all four cards in the player's hand to share a suit and scores 4 points; if the starter is also of that same suit, the flush scores 5. The crib is stricter: a crib flush only counts if all four crib cards AND the starter share the same suit, and in that case it scores 5. A four-card-only crib flush does not score.

entries.title: Counting: 'His Nobs'
entries.summary: If the player's hand (or the crib) contains a Jack whose suit matches the suit of the starter card, they score 1 point for 'His Nobs' — distinct from and in addition to the dealer's 2 for 'His Heels' when the starter itself is a Jack.

entries.title: Worked example: 8, 7, 7, 6, 2 scores 16
entries.summary: Given a five-card set of 8, 7, 7, 6, 2 (four hand cards plus starter): the fifteens are 8+7, 8+7, 7+6+2, and 7+6+2 (one 7 per combination), for four fifteens at 2 each (8 points). The two 7s form one pair (2 points). The runs 8-7-6 can be built two ways because either 7 can complete the sequence, for two runs of three (6 points). Total: 16 points.

worked_example.scenario: Hand of 8, 7, 7, 6, 2 counted with all four hand cards plus the starter
decomposition: Four fifteens from 8+7, 8+7, 7+6+2, and 7+6+2, one 7 per combination (8 points)
One pair from the two 7s (2 points)
Two runs of three from 8-7-6, one built with each 7 (6 points)

entries.title: Counting: common combined-formula shortcuts
entries.summary: Handy shortcuts for common combined patterns in a five-card show: three of a kind counts 6 (three pairs). Four of a kind counts 12 (six pairs). A three-card run with one rank duplicated (a 'double run') counts 8 (two runs of 3 plus a pair). A four-card run with one duplicated rank counts 10 (two runs of 4 plus a pair). A three-card run with one rank triplicated counts 15 (three runs of 3 plus a triplet). A three-card run with two different ranks duplicated counts 16 (four runs of 3 plus two pairs).

entries.title: The perfect 29 hand
entries.summary: The highest possible score in a single Cribbage show is 29 points. It requires the player to hold three 5s plus the Jack of some suit, with the starter being the fourth 5 of that same suit. The score decomposes as: four distinct 5+5+5 combinations for four fifteens (8 points), four distinct Jack+5 combinations for another four fifteens (8 points), double pair royal on the four 5s (12 points), and His Nobs on the Jack matching the starter's suit (1 point). Total 29.

worked_example.scenario: Hand of J-5-5-5 with the starter being the fourth 5, matching the Jack's suit
worked_example.expected_outcome: 29 points — the maximum possible score in a single Cribbage show
decomposition: Four fifteens from Jack+5 combinations (8 points)
Double pair royal on the four 5s (12 points)
His Nobs from the Jack matching the starter's suit (1 point)

entries.title: Play-phase vs show-phase scoring restrictions
entries.summary: Two important scope rules bridge the play and the show. First, the Ace always ranks low for run purposes; A-2-3 is a valid run in either phase, but Q-K-A is not. Second, flushes only count in the show, never in the play phase.

entries.title: Board mechanics: two pegs and 'twice around'
entries.summary: The board has four rows of 30 holes split into two per-player tracks, plus game holes at one end where the pegs start. Each player uses two pegs of one color. To record a score the rearmost peg leapfrogs the frontmost peg forward by the number of points scored, keeping the previous position visible for correction. Custom is to go 'down' (away from the game holes) on the outer row and 'up' the inner row; the standard 121-point game is 'twice around' the board.

entries.title: Lurch: winning before opponent reaches halfway
entries.summary: In the classic scoring convention, if the winner reaches 121 before the loser has reached the halfway mark of 61, the loser is 'lurched' and the winner is credited with two games instead of one. This is distinct from and older than the skunk rule; see the skunk variant entry for the more aggressive multipliers.

entries.title: Variant: Muggins ('claim missed points')
entries.summary: Under Muggins, players must announce their own scores aloud when counting a hand or the crib. Any points the counter fails to claim can be pointed out by the opponent, who calls 'Muggins!' and pegs those points themselves. Muggins must be agreed to before play begins; it is standard in most competitive Cribbage play.

entries.title: Variant: shorter game to 61
entries.summary: For a shorter session the game target is dropped to 61 points instead of 121. All other rules of the standard two-player game apply unchanged.

entries.title: Variant: skunk and double skunk
entries.summary: Under the skunk convention, if the losing player fails to reach 91 points by the end of the 121-point game, the winner is credited with a double game. If the loser fails to reach 61 points, the winner is credited with a quadruple game, called a 'double skunk'. This layers on top of, and is more punitive than, the older lurch convention.

entries.title: Strategy heuristic: crib discards
entries.summary: Advisory only. As dealer, discard cards that combine well in the crib but keep the strongest scoring cards in hand. As non-dealer, discard cards that are unlikely to help the dealer form 15s or runs — Aces and Kings tend to be safer to give up, while 5s, pairs, and adjacent-rank cards are the most dangerous discards.

entries.title: Strategy heuristic: leads and running-total traps
entries.summary: Advisory only. Leading a 5 is dangerous because any 10-value card makes 15 for the opponent. Leading a 4 is comparatively safe because it can't be immediately raised to 15 with a single card. Leading from a pair is often good if the matching partner is still in hand. Aces and 2s are usually held to help hit 15, 31, or salvage a Go. Try not to leave the running total sitting at 21 for the opponent — a 10-value response makes 31.
